solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

indicators.note: something awful is in a bad state, so these letters are knocked into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone sneers at a nasty rodent of a man who backs Spain.
explanation.definitionFit: A partisan is a committed adherent of a cause or party, a backer.

parts.note: so means very, as in 'so good'

explanation.surface: A soggy, aged settlement is described.
explanation.walkthrough: SOWETO is the large township near Johannesburg, South Africa.
explanation.definitionFit: Soweto is a famous South African township, an example of the definition.

indicators.note: nuts means crazy, so the letters of the preceding word go wild and rearrange

explanation.surface: Upmarket nuts are on sale in a shop.
explanation.walkthrough: 'nuts' looks like goods on the shelf but signals rearranging POSH.
explanation.definitionFit: A store and a shop are synonyms for a retail outlet.

definitions.meaning: a layered dessert, a sweet in British usage
something of little value or importance

explanation.surface: A tiny item is described as cute.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain 'a sweet' means a dessert course; trifle is sponge, fruit, custard and cream.
explanation.definitionFit: Trifle names both a British pudding and an insignificant matter.

clue.text: Swimming in water after ending in brook, jumpers say?

indicators.note: after places the anagram after the single letter taken from brook
the ending in a word is its last letter, so only the final letter of brook is used
swimming suggests the letters move freely around, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: Animals that jump are seen swimming after a brook ends.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Swimming' rearranges IN WATER to NITWEAR, placed after K. 'jumpers' are British sweaters, not leapers.
explanation.definitionFit: Jumpers (British for sweaters) are examples of knitted clothing, hence the question mark.

definitions.meaning: 'I ...!' is what one says when unable to find an answer

explanation.surface: Someone asked to surrender shrugs in confusion.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrasal verb means yield, and as an exclamation it concedes ignorance of an answer.

definitions.meaning: the past tense of leave, meaning went away

explanation.surface: One faction departed.
explanation.definitionFit: Left names a direction or side and is also the past tense of leave, departed.

clue.text: Different part of America: no, the reverse

indicators.note: part of says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A different region is sought: not America but its opposite.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the reverse' looks like a reversal instruction but is just part of the hiding text.
explanation.definitionFit: Another means a different one, as in 'try another way'.

indicators.note: installed means put in place, so the letter for one is set inside the facial feature

parts.note: the nose is a facial feature
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A sound system has one component fitted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'feature' is a facial feature, not a component.
explanation.definitionFit: Noise is a sound, typically a loud or unwanted one.

indicators.note: banishing means sending away, so the two letters are removed from the city's name

parts.note: Antwerp is a major port city in Belgium

explanation.surface: A Belgian city is expelling a fool.
explanation.definitionFit: A twerp is a silly or foolish person, an informal synonym.

clue.text: Darwin's survivors set it out in newspaper

indicators.note: in places the rearranged letters within the newspaper's initials

parts.note: FT is the Financial Times, a British newspaper

indicators.note: out means wrong or disordered, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A newspaper lays out an article on Darwin's theory.
explanation.walkthrough: FT is the Financial Times. 'Darwin's survivors' alludes to 'survival of the fittest'; 'out' signals the anagram and 'in' the insertion.
explanation.definitionFit: Darwin's theory is often summed up as 'survival of the fittest', so the fittest are those who survive.

clue.text: Penny I invested in bust we chose, artwork on display

indicators.note: invested in means put into, so the penny and I go inside the rearranged letters
bust means broken, so these letters are smashed and reassembled

explanation.surface: A collector puts money into a sculpted bust, picking the gallery's star piece.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bust' looks like a sculpture but rearranges WE CHOSE; P and I go inside.
explanation.definitionFit: A showpiece is an item displayed as an outstanding example, such as a prized work of art.

clue.text: Boy slips all over the place, perhaps

indicators.note: all over the place means scattered in disorder, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A boy keeps slipping everywhere, maybe.
explanation.definitionFit: Possibly and perhaps are synonyms expressing uncertainty.

clue.text: Young setter, maybe, changing nothing by going back?

definitions.meaning: a setter is a dog breed
a cryptic description of a palindrome: read backwards, this three-letter word is unchanged

explanation.surface: A junior crossword setter wonders whether retreating changes anything.
explanation.walkthrough: A setter here is the dog breed, not the puzzle compiler. The second half describes the answer itself, which reads the same either way.
explanation.definitionFit: A setter is a breed of dog, and a young dog is a puppy, so a juvenile setter fits.

clue.text: Equality inspires leaders on official list in opposition

indicators.note: inspires is read as breathes in, so the picked letters are taken inside the word for equality
leaders on the following words are their first letters

explanation.surface: A push for equality motivates officials heading the list of opponents.
explanation.walkthrough: 'inspires' literally means breathes in: OL goes into PARITY.
explanation.definitionFit: Polarity is the state of having opposed poles or tendencies, a contrast or opposition.

indicators.note: backing means going back, so the word for achieved is read in reverse

parts.note: won means achieved, as in 'won a prize'

explanation.surface: Support has been secured in the present day.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Backing' looks like support but signals reading WON backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Now and today both refer to the present time.

indicators.note: breaking suggests the words are broken up, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone got rich by committing crimes.
explanation.definitionFit: A fortune is a large amount of money, so wealth is a synonym.

indicators.note: dashed means smashed, so these letters are broken and rearranged

explanation.surface: A knight ran quickly around the chapel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Round' looks like a preposition; it is the adjective definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Spherical means shaped like a ball, the fullest sense of round.

clue.text: Embrace Cambridgeshire city in a big way

parts.note: Ely is a small cathedral city in Cambridgeshire, England

explanation.surface: Someone lovingly takes an English cathedral city to their heart.
explanation.walkthrough: ELY is a cathedral city near Cambridge in eastern England.
explanation.definitionFit: Hugely means to a very great extent, which is doing something in a big way.

definitions.meaning: an area of open public land, like a park

explanation.surface: A plain, unremarkable public park.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain a common is open land shared by a community, such as Clapham Common.
explanation.definitionFit: Common means usual or plain, and as a noun names public open land used like a park.

clue.text: Cold in head of boy going fast

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: A chill gets into a boy's head while he speeds along.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cold' looks like an illness the boy catches; it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Bracing weather or air is invigoratingly cold.

definitions.meaning: the visible swelling of a pregnant woman's belly
a light knock, as in a small car accident

explanation.surface: A small crash hints that something was anticipated.
explanation.definitionFit: A bump is a pregnancy belly and also a minor knock or crash.

clue.text: More dull, rug sent back by Queen

indicators.note: sent back means returned, so the word for rug is reversed

parts.note: a mat is a small rug
ER stands for Elizabeth Regina, Queen Elizabeth

explanation.surface: The Queen returns a duller rug.
explanation.definitionFit: Tame means bland or unexciting, so tamer is the comparative, duller.

definitions.meaning: a chalk-stream river in Hampshire, England

explanation.surface: An inspection of a Hampshire waterway.
explanation.walkthrough: Hampshire is a county in southern England; the Test is famous for fly fishing.
explanation.definitionFit: Test and check both mean examine; the Test is a named English river.

clue.text: Time to access food in tin, for example

indicators.note: to access means to get into, so the letter for time goes inside the word for food

parts.note: a meal is food eaten at one sitting

explanation.surface: It is time to get at the food in a tin can.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tin' looks like a can for food; it is the element.
explanation.definitionFit: Tin is one chemical element classed as a metal.

indicators.note: hugging means holding close, so the oaf's letters wrap around the tree

parts.note: a lout is an oaf, a clumsy boor
the ash is a common tree

explanation.surface: An environmentalist lout embracing trees gets attacked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tree-hugging' suggests an eco-activist; here LOUT literally hugs ASH.
explanation.definitionFit: To lash out is to strike suddenly, verbally or physically, an idiom for attacking.
